answer.label: Not verifiably Tesla — a secondhand recollection
answer.sourceLine: No patent, lecture, article, letter or interview by Tesla has ever been produced containing this sentence. Wikiquote files it under “Disputed,” and the only named source is an undated web page by Ralph Bergstresser — a man who sold Tesla-branded “purple plates” — recalling a private conversation he dated to 1942.

source.heading: What the record actually shows

docMeta.dd: Comments From the Inventor of the Purple Harmony Plates
Ralph Bergstresser (1912–1998), seller of Tesla-branded “purple plates”; page undated
A private conversation Bergstresser said he had with Tesla in 1942
No patent, lecture, article or letter with this wording has ever been produced

source.excerpt: If you want to find the secrets of the universe, think in terms of energy, frequency and vibration. My brain is only a receiver, in the Universe there is a core from which we obtain knowledge, strength and inspiration. I have not penetrated into the secrets of this core, but I know that it exists.
trail: Wikiquote places the line in its “Disputed” section, and it is the only entry there. The citation reads: “Quoted by Ralph Bergstresser, who claimed to have heard this from Tesla in person” — pointing at a page on bibliotecapleyades.net, with no date given (Wikiquote, Nikola Tesla ↗).

The cited page is Bergstresser’s own sales literature. It carries the sentence “If you want to find the secrets of the Universe, think in terms of energy, frequency and vibration” and frames it as coming from “a conversation with the famous scientist, Dr. Nikola Tesla, in 1942” — a recollection, decades after the fact, by a man marketing Tesla-branded plates (Comments From the Inventor of the Purple Harmony Plates ↗).

Wikiquote’s editors searched and came up empty. On the talk page, editor Salimfadhley wrote in December 2015: “Has anybody managed to find a source for this quote? It has been quoted hundreds of times in all kinds of spiritual texts, but I’ve never seen it published in any primary source or in any contemporary record.” Editor Fountains of Bryn Mawr cautioned that quotes sourced to someone selling a product should be discounted; Salimfadhley then added the line to the “Disputed” section, saying it was worth preserving because the misquote “seems to be so widely used in pseudoscience” (5 December 2015 — Talk:Nikola Tesla ↗).

What Tesla verifiably wrote sounds different. His genuine Century Magazine essay of June 1900 uses the vocabulary in an engineering register — “currents of extremely high frequency or rate of vibration,” a circuit “adjusted, or ‘tuned,’ exactly to electrical vibrations of the proper kind” — never as a key to the secrets of the universe (The Problem of Increasing Human Energy ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is the full entry as Wikiquote records it, in its Disputed section — the famous first sentence usually circulates detached from the “my brain is only a receiver” continuation. Neither half has been traced to anything Tesla wrote or published.
source.rightsNote: Rights cannot be assessed, because the wording’s origin is unknown. It is not traceable to any published work by Tesla, so no Tesla-era publication date applies. The only named carrier is an undated web page by Ralph Bergstresser (who died in 1998) — and it is not established that he coined the sentence rather than repeated it. Quotle asserts no copyright status here; do not assume this line is in the public domain.

author.name: Nikola Tesla
author.kicker: The man it is pinned on
author.heading: Who Tesla actually was
author.bio: Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 – 7 January 1943) was, in Wikipedia’s words, a Serbian-American engineer, futurist, and inventor, best known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating-current supply system. He genuinely spent his career on frequency, oscillation and resonance — his 1900 Century Magazine essay talks about “currents of extremely high frequency or rate of vibration” and circuits “tuned” to electrical vibrations. That real technical vocabulary is exactly what makes the disputed line so hard to dislodge: it sounds like something he plausibly could have said. He died in New York City in January 1943.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Tesla
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook Tesla magnet quote: a spiritual-sounding aphorism attached to a scientist famous enough to make it sound authoritative. The attribution chain has exactly one link, and that link has a commercial interest in it.

items.why: Nothing Tesla published contains it. Wikiquote lists it in Disputed rather than among his sourced quotations, on the strength of a single secondhand claim (Wikiquote ↗).

Bergstresser’s page presents the line as Tesla’s words from “a conversation with the famous scientist, Dr. Nikola Tesla, in 1942” — in his own promotional text, reproduced on the alternative-topics archive bibliotecapleyades.net (bibliotecapleyades.net ↗). Wikiquote’s editors specifically flagged that quotations sourced to someone selling a product should be discounted (Talk:Nikola Tesla ↗).

The famous sentence is normally quoted alone, but Wikiquote’s disputed entry continues: “My brain is only a receiver, in the Universe there is a core from which we obtain knowledge, strength and inspiration.” Both halves rest on the same single unverified claim (Wikiquote ↗).

The line reached Wikiquote’s attention through consumer products: the talk-page thread was opened in 2014 by an editor who had seen it on wall decals and wanted it verified. It now circulates on posters, stickers and shareable images, none of which carry a citation (Talk:Nikola Tesla ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is not “Tesla said it” and not “someone else said it” — it is that nobody has produced a source. One man, selling Tesla-branded plates, said Tesla told him so in private; Wikiquote records that claim and marks it Disputed ↗. Until a letter, a transcript or a contemporary account turns up, that is all there is.

context.heading: Why this one sticks
lead: The quote is unusually sticky because it is almost in character. Tesla really did spend his life on oscillation, resonance and frequency, and he really did write in those words — his June 1900 essay in Century Magazine, “The Problem of Increasing Human Energy,” describes “currents of extremely high frequency or rate of vibration” and a receiving circuit “adjusted, or ‘tuned,’ exactly to electrical vibrations of the proper kind.” A reader who knows that vocabulary hears the disputed line and thinks: yes, that is him.

But the register is wrong. In Tesla’s documented prose, frequency and vibration are engineering parameters — things you tune a circuit to, or drive nitrogen with. In the disputed line they are a metaphysical master key. That shift, from apparatus to cosmology, is the signature of the community the sentence actually comes from: the New Age and “free energy” literature in which Bergstresser sold his plates.
detailsBody: A fair point in the quote’s favour: the claimed date is not impossible. Tesla died in New York City on 7 January 1943, so a conversation in 1942 falls inside his lifetime. Bergstresser’s vendor biography says he was born in 1912 in Pueblo, Colorado, met Tesla, and had “numerous conversations” with him; he died in 1998.

What is missing is any corroboration. There is no letter, no notebook entry, no contemporary press account, and no second witness. The claim surfaces only in material written to sell a product, and it is the sort of line — quotable, flattering, cosmically ambitious — that a marketer has every incentive to remember generously. That is why Wikiquote kept it but flagged it, rather than treating it as sourced.
context.pull: Tesla wrote about vibration as something you tune a circuit to. The quote treats it as a key to the universe.
